claim_text: A heart is placed on a scale. On the other side sits a symbol of what is right and true. Standing beside the scale is a god with the head of a canine: Anubis. He is famous as the fearsome judge of the dead. But look closely at the ancient sources, and you will find that Anubis does not judge alone.

source_locations: Description, artwork details, museum audio transcript;Description; Spell 125 scene; date; museum audio transcript
claim_text: So what was Anubis actually doing? Watching over tombs, protecting the bodies of the dead, guiding them on their journey, and checking the scale that weighs the heart. In this episode, we follow sculptures and papyri at The Metropolitan Museum of Art to see, one by one, the work Anubis does in the sources.

source_locations: Description, artwork details, museum audio transcript;Description; Spell 125 scene; date; museum audio transcript;Artist, medium, facsimile dimensions, original location and credit line
claim_text: On screen you will see photographs of real museum objects, along with reconstructions created to help you picture the past. Every reconstruction is labeled in the top corner. Let's begin with the first object.

source_locations: Description, artwork details, museum audio transcript
claim_text: First, this statue of a reclining canine. Its front legs stretch forward and its ears stand upright. It seems less asleep than alert, keeping watch. This statue at the Met is carved from limestone and was originally painted black. The god was not always shown in human form.

source_locations: Description, artwork details, museum audio transcript
claim_text: The museum's description draws attention to the link between canines and cemeteries. Animals that roamed burial grounds could disturb the dead. Yet a watchful canine could also be imagined as a power that guarded them. This is an interpretation of the image's background, not proof of a single origin for Anubis.

source_locations: Description and artwork details; identification marked probable
claim_text: In another statuette, an animal head sits on a human body. It is made of wood, and fine details of the clothing still survive. The museum describes it as probably Anubis, because more than one god was shown with a canine head. A familiar look does not always tell us the name for certain.

source_locations: Description, artwork details, museum audio transcript;Description and artwork details; identification marked probable;Description of royal ritual and ankh; object date and museum audio transcript
claim_text: This is where dates matter. The statues we have just seen and the royal relief we will see later were not made in the same era. Ancient Egypt covers an enormous span of time. To understand a god's form and role, we need to ask not only what is depicted, but when the object was made.

source_locations: Nedjemankh Becomes a Mummy; burial rites and embalming scene
claim_text: One of Anubis's most important roles was his connection to mummification. In ancient belief, preparing the body of the deceased and performing rituals helped sustain their existence after death. Preserving the body was not only about appearance. It was tied to the hope of living again.

source_locations: Nedjemankh Becomes a Mummy; burial rites and embalming scene;Press release, February 2019: coffin of Nedjemankh returned to Egypt after it was found to have been looted in 2011
claim_text: A gilded coffin made for a priest named Nedjemankh was once displayed at the Met. The museum's description points to a scene of a mummy on a bier, with Anubis performing rites beside it. Isis and Nephthys also appear as protectors of the mummy. The coffin was later found to have been looted, and in 2019 it was returned to Egypt.

source_locations: Description, artwork details, museum audio transcript;Nedjemankh Becomes a Mummy; burial rites and embalming scene
claim_text: Of course, it was living people who prepared the dead and readied them for burial. The stories of the gods gave meaning to that work. Human hands and divine protection: together, they shaped the funerary rites.

source_locations: Description of shrine, protective placement and funerary rites
claim_text: The idea of protection appears beyond statues of the god, too. The ritual object called an imiut combines a staff, a jar, and a form wrapped in an animal skin. According to the museum, objects like this and guardian figures were connected to sacred spaces and funerary rites. Protecting the dead took many forms.

source_locations: Description; Spell 125 scene; date; museum audio transcript
claim_text: Now we move from preparing the body to the story of the journey after death. Here we meet the Book of the Dead. The museum notes that its ancient name was the Book of Going Forth by Day. It is a collection of spells and images on papyrus, meant to help the deceased on their way.

source_locations: Description; Spell 125 scene; date; museum audio transcript
claim_text: On screen now is a papyrus that accompanied the burial of a woman named Nauny. The museum dates it to around 1050 BCE. The scroll holds images and texts for several spells, and among them is the scene of the weighing of the heart. It was made not for an abstract dead person, but for one particular individual.

source_locations: Description of heart, Maat, Thoth, Anubis and Ammut; artwork details
claim_text: Why the heart? Writing about another funerary papyrus, the museum explains that the heart was considered the center of intellect and emotion. In the weighing scene, how a person had lived is what is being tested. The heart was shown not as a mere organ, but as a record of a life.

source_locations: Description; Spell 125 scene; date; museum audio transcript;Description of heart, Maat, Thoth, Anubis and Ammut; artwork details
claim_text: On the other side of the scale is something representing Maat. Maat is linked to order and to what is right. Many people picture only a feather, but in Nauny's papyrus, Maat appears as a small goddess wearing a feather. It is worth remembering that one famous image does not fit every source.

source_locations: Artist, medium, facsimile dimensions, original location and credit line
claim_text: Here is another scene of Anubis and the scale. But this image is not a photograph of the ancient wall painting itself. It is a copy on paper, made by Nina de Garis Davies from the tomb of Nakhtamun. It is a valuable way to study the imagery, but we present the original and the copy as different things.

source_locations: Description; Spell 125 scene; date; museum audio transcript
claim_text: Let's look again at Nauny's papyrus. Anubis is reading the scale. But he is not alone in the scene. There is a god who records the result, and a god who receives the dead. Once we separate these roles, the idea of Anubis as a judge who decides everything on his own turns out to be too simple.

source_locations: Description and Roman-period date; placement of gods
claim_text: On this fragment of cartonnage, Thoth, with the head of an ibis, holds writing equipment. The museum describes the scene as Thoth introducing the deceased to Osiris. The clue to identifying a god is not just the shape of the head. What the god holds, and what the god is doing, matter just as much.

source_locations: Description of heart, Maat, Thoth, Anubis and Ammut; artwork details
claim_text: According to the museum, if the scale balanced, the deceased was accepted by Osiris and granted eternal life. If not, the heart was devoured by a creature called Ammut, and the person died forever. Anubis weighs, Thoth records, Osiris receives. Judgment was pictured as a scene involving many gods.

source_locations: Description; Spell 125 scene; date; museum audio transcript;Description of heart, Maat, Thoth, Anubis and Ammut; artwork details
claim_text: The judgment scene does have its frightening side. But the sources prepared for the dead were not about failure alone. They were about passing the test safely and moving on to the next existence. Seen through his role as a protector, the same scene of the scale begins to look a little different.

source_locations: Description of royal ritual and ankh; object date and museum audio transcript
claim_text: Now for a somewhat unexpected object: a relief showing King Amenemhat I. On either side of the king stand Horus and Anubis, offering him the ankh, the sign of life. The museum connects this scene to royal ritual. Anubis appears in more places than the weighing of the heart.

source_locations: Description of royal ritual and ankh; object date and museum audio transcript
claim_text: Here the king demonstrates, through ritual, that even after a long reign he still has the power to rule. Anubis was connected to this place in his role as lord of the necropolis. The relief dates to around 1980 BCE. Set beside later statues, it shows how the same god was spoken of across a very long span of time.

source_locations: Description and Roman-period date; placement of gods
claim_text: Much later, Anubis also appears on a fragment of cartonnage from the Roman period. Osiris sits at the center, with Thoth and other gods nearby. Long after, the relationship between the dead and the gods was still being depicted. Still, we need not treat each object as a copy of exactly the same story.

source_locations: Description explicitly leaves identity uncertain; Roman-period date
claim_text: For this small gold figure, the museum offers two readings: it may be Anubis, or it may be another god. The museum states clearly that its identity is uncertain. Leaving the unknown as unknown is part of telling history honestly. A sharp image does not make an explanation certain.

source_locations: Object title, bronze/cupreous alloy, 7.7 cm height, date and credit line
claim_text: Beyond large paintings and statues, there is also a figure of Anubis only about 7.7 centimeters tall, made of bronze or copper alloy. Exploring museum collections shows that grand myths were also expressed in objects small enough to hold in your hand. Who used it, where, and how? Small objects open up new questions.

source_locations: Description, artwork details, museum audio transcript;Nedjemankh Becomes a Mummy; burial rites and embalming scene;Description; Spell 125 scene; date; museum audio transcript
claim_text: Anubis was shown watching over tombs, took part in the rites that prepared the body, and appears in the weighing of the heart. He is a god deeply bound to death, but his role cannot be summed up by fear alone. Protecting, and helping the dead pass their test: the sources let us read him as a god involved in both.

source_locations: Description; Spell 125 scene; date; museum audio transcript;Description of heart, Maat, Thoth, Anubis and Ammut; artwork details
claim_text: From the story of the heart preserved on papyrus, we can take away a question. If you could carry something beyond death, what part of you would say who you were? Behind the images of the gods, we can see people's wish to support the dead on their journey.
